title: Donoghue v Stevenson
facts: Mrs Donoghue drank ginger beer bought for her by a friend in a Paisley café. The bottle was opaque, and she says it contained the remains of a decomposed snail.
why: This is the birth of the modern law of negligence.

title: Caparo Industries plc v Dickman
facts: Caparo bought shares in Fidelity plc and then took the company over, relying on audited accounts that turned out to overstate its profits. Caparo sued the auditors for negligent misstatement.
why: Caparo replaced the expansive approach of Anns v Merton with a three-stage test for novel duty situations: was the harm reasonably foreseeable, was there a relationship of proximity between the parties, and is it fair, just and reasonable to impose a duty?

title: Hedley Byrne & Co Ltd v Heller & Partners Ltd
facts: An advertising agency asked its bank to check the creditworthiness of a client. The client's bankers, Heller, gave a favourable reference 'without responsibility'.
why: Before Hedley Byrne, negligence generally compensated only physical injury and property damage.

title: Rylands v Fletcher
facts: Rylands built a reservoir on his land. Unknown to him, disused mine shafts ran beneath it, and when the reservoir filled the water burst through into Fletcher's neighbouring colliery and flooded it.
why: Rylands v Fletcher is the leading example of strict liability in English tort law — liability without proof of fault.

title: Montgomery v Lanarkshire Health Board
facts: Mrs Montgomery, a diabetic woman of small stature, was not told about the roughly 10% risk of shoulder dystocia during a vaginal delivery, nor offered a caesarean. Her son suffered severe injuries during birth.
why: Montgomery moved English medical law decisively from paternalism to patient autonomy.

title: Robinson v Chief Constable of West Yorkshire Police
facts: Two police officers tried to arrest a suspected drug dealer on a busy Huddersfield street. In the struggle they knocked over Mrs Robinson, a 76-year-old passer-by, and injured her.
why: Robinson clarified two things.

title: Carlill v Carbolic Smoke Ball Co
facts: The Carbolic Smoke Ball Company advertised that it would pay £100 to anyone who used its smoke ball as directed and still caught influenza, adding that £1,000 had been deposited with a bank 'showing our sincerity in the matter'. Mrs Carlill used the ball, caught flu, and claimed the reward.
why: Carlill is the classic introduction to offer and acceptance.

title: Balfour v Balfour
facts: Mr Balfour worked in Ceylon (now Sri Lanka). When his wife stayed in England for medical reasons he promised to pay her £30 a month.
why: Balfour established 'intention to create legal relations' as a requirement of a binding contract, alongside offer, acceptance and consideration.

title: Central London Property Trust Ltd v High Trees House Ltd
facts: In 1937 High Trees leased a block of London flats at £2,500 a year. When the war left the flats half-empty, the landlord agreed in 1940 to halve the rent.
why: High Trees launched the modern doctrine of promissory estoppel: where one party makes a clear promise intended to be relied upon, and the other relies on it, the promisor may be prevented from going back on it even without consideration.

title: Hadley v Baxendale
facts: The crankshaft in Hadley's Gloucester flour mill broke. He engaged Baxendale's carriers to take it to the makers as a pattern for a new one.
why: Hadley v Baxendale sets the rule on remoteness of damage in contract that every law student learns in their first term.

title: Williams v Roffey Bros & Nicholls (Contractors) Ltd
facts: Roffey, the main contractor refurbishing a block of flats, subcontracted the carpentry to Williams for £20,000. Williams ran into financial trouble and was behind schedule.
why: Williams v Roffey reshaped the doctrine of consideration.

title: Patel v Mirza
facts: Mr Patel gave Mr Mirza £620,000 to bet on the share price of a bank using inside information — a criminal scheme. The insider information never arrived, the bets were never placed, and Mirza kept the money.
why: Patel v Mirza is a landmark on the defence of illegality, but it is most interesting as a debate about legal method.

title: R v Dudley and Stephens
facts: After the yacht Mignonette sank in the South Atlantic, four crew members drifted in an open boat for weeks with almost no food or water. Dudley and Stephens killed the cabin boy, Richard Parker, who was the weakest and closest to death, and the three survivors ate him until they were rescued.
why: Dudley and Stephens is the foundational case on necessity and one of the most discussed cases in legal philosophy.

title: R v Brown
facts: A group of adult men took part in consensual sadomasochistic activities in private. Nobody complained to the police, no one needed medical treatment, and the activities came to light only through a video.
why: Brown is the leading case on the limits of consent in the criminal law, and a classic battleground between two views of what criminal law is for.

title: R v R
facts: A husband was charged with attempting to rape his wife, from whom he had separated. He relied on a statement by the eighteenth-century jurist Sir Matthew Hale that a husband could not be guilty of raping his wife because by marrying she had given irrevocable consent.
why: R v R shows judges abolishing a long-standing rule because it had become morally indefensible — a striking example of the common law changing without Parliament.

title: R v Woollin
facts: Woollin lost his temper and threw his three-month-old son onto a hard surface, fracturing the baby's skull and killing him. He said he had not intended to kill or seriously injure the child.
why: Woollin fixes the meaning of 'oblique' or indirect intention in English criminal law and shows how carefully the law distinguishes murder (which requires intention) from manslaughter (which does not).

title: R v Jogee
facts: Jogee was outside a house shouting encouragement while his friend Hirsi stabbed and killed a man inside. Under the then law of 'joint enterprise', a secondary party could be convicted of murder if he merely foresaw that the principal might intentionally kill or cause serious harm.
why: Jogee is a rare example of the Supreme Court openly declaring that the law had been wrong for decades and correcting it — and of campaigning by families and the group JENGbA influencing the development of the law.

title: Ivey v Genting Casinos (UK) Ltd
facts: Phil Ivey, a professional gambler, won £7.7 million at Crockfords casino playing punto banco using 'edge-sorting' — persuading the croupier to rotate cards so he could read tiny asymmetries in their backs. The casino refused to pay, saying he had cheated.
why: Although Ivey was a civil case about a gambling contract, its obiter comments on dishonesty were later confirmed as the law by the Court of Appeal in R v Barton and Booth (2020).

title: Entick v Carrington
facts: Agents of the Secretary of State broke into John Entick's house, searched it for four hours and carried away his papers, acting under a general warrant that named no specific offence. Entick sued for trespass.
why: Entick v Carrington is the founding case of the rule of law in the English constitution.

title: Associated Provincial Picture Houses Ltd v Wednesbury Corporation
facts: Wednesbury Corporation granted a cinema a licence for Sunday opening on condition that no children under fifteen were admitted. The cinema argued the condition was unreasonable.
why: 'Wednesbury unreasonableness' is the classic standard of review in administrative law and a word every public lawyer uses.

title: Ridge v Baldwin
facts: The Chief Constable of Brighton was acquitted of conspiracy to obstruct the course of justice but was heavily criticised by the trial judge. The Watch Committee dismissed him without giving him notice of the charges or a chance to respond.
why: Ridge v Baldwin revived the rules of natural justice — the right to a fair hearing and the rule against bias — and applied them to administrative decision-makers generally, not just to courts.

title: Anisminic Ltd v Foreign Compensation Commission
facts: Anisminic's property in Egypt was seized during the Suez crisis. The Foreign Compensation Commission rejected its claim on a misreading of the rules.
why: Anisminic is the leading authority on the courts' refusal to let Parliament shut them out of reviewing unlawful executive action.

title: Council of Civil Service Unions v Minister for the Civil Service (the GCHQ case)
facts: Margaret Thatcher, as Minister for the Civil Service, used the royal prerogative to ban staff at GCHQ, the government's intelligence communications centre, from belonging to trade unions, without consulting them. The unions sought judicial review.
why: The GCHQ case is important twice over.

title: Pepper (Inspector of Taxes) v Hart
facts: Teachers at Malvern College could send their sons to the school for a fifth of the normal fees. The Revenue said the benefit should be taxed on the full cost of a place; the teachers said it should be taxed on the marginal cost, which was almost nothing.
why: Pepper v Hart is the key case on statutory interpretation and the use of parliamentary materials.

title: Thoburn v Sunderland City Council (the 'Metric Martyrs' case)
facts: Steven Thoburn, a Sunderland greengrocer, was prosecuted for selling bananas by the pound rather than in metric units, as required by regulations made under the European Communities Act 1972. He argued that a later Act, the Weights and Measures Act 1985, had impliedly repealed the 1972 Act to the extent they conflicted.
why: Thoburn introduced the idea of a hierarchy of statutes into a constitution that famously has no single written document.

title: R (Miller) v Secretary of State for Exiting the European Union
facts: After the 2016 referendum, the government proposed to give notice of the UK's withdrawal from the EU under Article 50 using the royal prerogative to conduct foreign affairs, without a vote in Parliament. Gina Miller challenged this.
why: Miller (No 1) is the most important constitutional decision of the twenty-first century so far.

title: R (Miller) v The Prime Minister; Cherry v Advocate General for Scotland
facts: In August 2019, with the Brexit deadline approaching, Prime Minister Boris Johnson advised the Queen to prorogue (suspend) Parliament for five weeks. Challenges were brought in England and Scotland.
why: Miller (No 2) shows the courts identifying and enforcing unwritten constitutional principles against the head of the executive.

title: R (UNISON) v Lord Chancellor
facts: In 2013 the government introduced fees of up to £1,200 to bring a claim in the employment tribunal, where previously claims had been free. The number of claims fell by around 70%.
why: UNISON is the leading modern statement that access to the courts is a constitutional right inherent in the rule of law, not merely a service the state may ration.

title: R (Evans) v Attorney General
facts: A Guardian journalist asked under the Freedom of Information Act to see letters written by Prince Charles to government ministers. The Upper Tribunal ordered disclosure after a full hearing.
why: Evans is a striking modern application of the rule of law and the separation of powers.

title: Reference by the Lord Advocate on the Scottish Independence Referendum Bill
facts: The Scottish Government wanted to hold a second independence referendum without Westminster's agreement. The Lord Advocate asked the Supreme Court whether the Scottish Parliament had power to legislate for one.
why: This case is the clearest modern explanation of how devolution works in law: the devolved legislatures are creatures of statute with limited competence, and the courts police the boundaries.

title: A v Secretary of State for the Home Department (the Belmarsh case)
facts: After the 11 September attacks, Parliament allowed the Home Secretary to detain foreign nationals suspected of terrorism indefinitely without trial if they could not be deported. Nine detainees held at Belmarsh prison challenged the scheme.
why: Belmarsh is the high point of the Human Rights Act 1998 in action.

title: Ghaidan v Godin-Mendoza
facts: Mr Godin-Mendoza had lived with his same-sex partner, the tenant of a flat, for many years. When his partner died, the landlord argued that he could not succeed to the tenancy because the Rent Act 1977 protected only a person living with the tenant 'as his or her wife or husband'.
why: Ghaidan is the leading case on section 3 of the Human Rights Act, which requires courts to read legislation compatibly with Convention rights 'so far as it is possible to do so'.

title: Airedale NHS Trust v Bland
facts: Tony Bland was crushed in the Hillsborough stadium disaster in 1989 and left in a persistent vegetative state, with no awareness and no prospect of recovery. His doctors and family wanted to withdraw the artificial feeding that kept him alive.
why: Bland is the foundation of English law on withdrawing life-sustaining treatment and remains the starting point for every end-of-life case.

title: Re A (Children) (Conjoined Twins: Surgical Separation)
facts: Jodie and Mary were conjoined twins. Mary's heart and lungs did not work; she survived only because she shared Jodie's circulation.
why: Re A is one of the hardest cases in English law, and the three judges reached the same result by strikingly different routes.

title: R (Nicklinson) v Ministry of Justice
facts: Tony Nicklinson suffered a stroke that left him with locked-in syndrome, able to communicate only by blinking. He wanted a doctor to be allowed to help him die.
why: Nicklinson is a study in institutional competence: which body — Parliament or the courts — should decide profound moral questions where society is divided?

title: Lee v Ashers Baking Company Ltd
facts: Mr Lee ordered a cake from a Belfast bakery iced with the message 'Support Gay Marriage'. The bakery's owners, who are Christians, refused because they objected to the message.
why: The 'gay cake' case is the leading UK authority on the collision between equality law and freedom of conscience and expression.

title: R (Begum) v Special Immigration Appeals Commission
facts: Shamima Begum left London aged fifteen to join Islamic State in Syria. In 2019 the Home Secretary deprived her of British citizenship on national security grounds.
why: Begum raises hard questions about citizenship, statelessness, the treatment of a person who was a child when she left, and how much deference courts should give the executive on security matters.

title: R (AAA (Syria)) v Secretary of State for the Home Department (the Rwanda case)
facts: The government's policy was to send certain asylum seekers to Rwanda to have their claims decided there. Claimants argued Rwanda was not a safe country.
why: The Rwanda case is a modern illustration of the rule of law meeting immigration politics.

title: For Women Scotland Ltd v The Scottish Ministers
facts: Scottish legislation aimed to increase the proportion of women on public boards, and Scottish Ministers' guidance said that a trans woman with a gender recognition certificate counted as a woman for that purpose. For Women Scotland challenged the guidance.
why: This is a landmark of statutory interpretation with major practical consequences for single-sex services, sport and employment.

title: Salomon v A Salomon & Co Ltd
facts: Aron Salomon, a successful leather merchant, turned his business into a limited company, taking almost all the shares himself and lending the company money secured by debentures. The company later failed.
why: Salomon is the cornerstone of company law.

title: Brown v Board of Education of Topeka
court: Supreme Court of the United States
facts: Linda Brown, a Black schoolgirl in Kansas, was refused a place at the white school near her home under laws segregating public schools by race. A unanimous Supreme Court, led by Chief Justice Earl Warren, held that racially segregated schools violate the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment.
why: Brown is the most celebrated decision of the US Supreme Court and a touchstone for arguments about whether courts can and should drive social change.

title: Marbury v Madison
court: Supreme Court of the United States
facts: In the last hours of his presidency John Adams appointed William Marbury as a justice of the peace, but the new administration under Thomas Jefferson refused to deliver his commission. Marbury asked the Supreme Court to order the Secretary of State, James Madison, to hand it over.
why: Marbury established judicial review in the American sense: the power of courts to strike down legislation that conflicts with the Constitution.
